Mrs. Dalia, 55, was admitted with pneumonia. She takes sertraline for depression and ondansetron for nausea. Her potassium was 3.2 mmol/L and magnesium low.

Her ECG showed a QTc of 510 milliseconds. Dr. Marwan started IV ceftriaxone. On the second day, because she was still coughing, he added azithromycin.

She had been coughing for a week and her chest X-ray showed a patch on the right. Her temperature was 38.1°C. She had a history of fainting once two years ago, which was put down to dehydration. She was frightened of being in hospital and asked for her sister to stay with her.

He also asked the nurses to replace her potassium and magnesium, and continued her sertraline because she said it helped her a lot. He asked for a daily ECG and asked her to call the nurse if she felt her heart flutter. He let her sister visit outside visiting hours.
h: he added azithromycin

a.o: Dr. Marwan added azithromycin to a woman with a QTc of 510 who was also on ondansetron.
a.x: He should have chosen an antibiotic that does not lengthen the QT, like doxycycline.
a.w: Azithromycin and ondansetron both lengthen the QT. A QTc over 500 with low potassium and magnesium risks torsades, a deadly rhythm.

a.o: Dr. Marwan replaced her potassium and magnesium.
a.x: The salts did not need fixing.
a.w: Low potassium and magnesium raise the risk of dangerous rhythms.

a.o: Dr. Marwan kept her antidepressant going.
a.x: Her sertraline should have been stopped.
a.w: Sertraline has very little effect on the QT, and stopping it suddenly can bring back her depression.

a.o: Dr. Marwan let her sister visit outside hours.
a.x: Visits must keep to the rules.
a.w: Flexible visits help patients recover.

s:
Mrs. Nesma, 33, has familial high cholesterol. Her LDL is 6.8 mmol/L and her father had a heart attack at 45. She came to clinic to start treatment.

While talking, she mentioned she was 10 weeks pregnant with her second child, and her pregnancy scan had been normal.

Her first child, a girl of four, is healthy. She has small yellow lumps on her Achilles tendons, which Dr. Raafat noticed. She does not smoke and her blood pressure was 112/70. Her thyroid and liver tests were normal. She asked if the cholesterol could harm her baby.

Dr. Raafat told her that her cholesterol was very high and started rosuvastatin 20 mg daily. He referred her children for cholesterol testing and told her to eat less saturated fat. He booked her back in three months for a blood test and liver tests and congratulated her on the pregnancy.
h: started rosuvastatin 20 mg daily

a.o: Dr. Raafat started a statin in a pregnant woman.
a.x: Statins should have waited until after pregnancy and breastfeeding.
a.w: Statins are not used in pregnancy because of possible harm to the baby. A few months without treatment carry little risk.

a.o: Dr. Raafat referred her children for cholesterol tests.
a.x: Children don't need cholesterol tests.
a.w: Familial hypercholesterolemia is inherited, so children should be tested.

a.o: Dr. Raafat gave diet advice to a pregnant woman.
a.x: Diet changes are unsafe in pregnancy.
a.w: Cutting saturated fat is safe and healthy in pregnancy.

a.o: Dr. Raafat booked liver tests.
a.x: Liver tests were not needed.
a.w: Liver tests are standard when starting lipid treatment.

s:
Mr. Waleed, 41, came to clinic with three weeks of fevers, night sweats and losing weight. He had a dental extraction a month ago. He has a known bicuspid aortic valve.

Dr. Asmaa heard a new murmur of aortic regurgitation. She noticed small painless red spots on his palms and tiny lines under his nails.

He is a teacher, doesn't smoke and doesn't use drugs. He had lost 4 kg in a month. His temperature in clinic was 38.2°C and his pulse 102. His spleen was just felt below his ribs. He had no cough and his urine dipstick showed a little blood.

She thought he had a viral illness and gave him a course of amoxicillin "in case". She booked an echo in four weeks and asked him to come back if his fever got worse. She told him not to go back to the dentist for now and checked his tetanus status, which was up to date.
h: gave him a course of amoxicillin "in case". She booked an echo in four weeks

a.o: Dr. Asmaa gave blind antibiotics and delayed an echo in a man with a valve problem, fever, a new murmur and skin signs.
a.x: Mr. Waleed should have had three blood cultures before any antibiotics and an urgent echo for endocarditis.
a.w: Fever plus a new murmur and skin spots mean endocarditis. Blind antibiotics can mask the cause; it needs proper cultures and weeks of IV treatment.

a.o: Dr. Asmaa told him not to go back to the dentist for now.
a.x: He should have gone back to the dentist.
a.w: Avoiding new dental work until the infection is known is sensible.

a.o: Dr. Asmaa checked his tetanus status.
a.x: That was irrelevant.
a.w: Checking tetanus is routine; it causes no harm.

a.o: Dr. Asmaa examined his hands.
a.x: Hands are not important for heart problems.
a.w: Hand signs help diagnose endocarditis.

s:
Mr. Medhat, 64, collapsed in the waiting room. He was not breathing and had no pulse. The team started CPR at once and attached the defibrillator.

The monitor showed a flat line with no electrical activity. Dr. Noha asked for adrenaline 1 mg and checked the leads; they were connected, the gain was up and the flat line was seen in two leads.

He had come in with indigestion an hour earlier and was waiting to be seen. A nurse had noticed him slumped in his chair. He was 64, with high blood pressure, and his son said he had been under stress at work. The team took turns doing compressions every two minutes.

She then delivered a 200-joule shock "in case it was fine VF" and continued CPR. She asked a nurse to time the cycles and another to look for reversible causes. She asked his son to step outside but let him come back when he asked to be present.
h: She then delivered a 200-joule shock "in case it was fine VF"

a.o: Dr. Noha shocked a flat line (asystole) after checking the leads.
a.x: She should have continued CPR and adrenaline without shocks for asystole.
a.w: Asystole is not a shockable rhythm. Shocking wastes time away from compressions.

a.o: Dr. Noha gave adrenaline straight away for asystole.
a.x: Adrenaline should wait until after the second shock.
a.w: In asystole adrenaline is given as soon as possible.

a.o: Dr. Noha checked the leads and gain.
a.x: This wasted time.
a.w: Checking leads makes sure the flat line is real.

a.o: Dr. Noha let his son come back into the room.
a.x: Families should never watch CPR.
a.w: Many families want to be present, and studies show it helps them.

t: Syncope from a heart block missed
s:
Mrs. Shadia, 78, fainted three times in a month without warning, once while sitting watching TV. She has no chest pain. Her pulse was 46 and regular.

Her ECG showed P waves that were not linked to the QRS complexes, with wide QRS complexes. Her blood tests, including potassium, were normal. She takes no heart-slowing drugs.

She lives alone and her neighbor found her on the floor after the last faint, with a bruise on her forehead. She had no warning before each faint and felt fine afterwards. She drinks plenty of water and takes only a calcium tablet. Her blood pressure was 148/70 lying and standing.

Her daughter, who visits on weekends, said her mother had been forgetting to drink during the hot weeks and that her urine looked dark. Mrs. Shadia had no new medicines and had not been ill. Dr. Gamal thought she was dehydrated from the summer heat. He advised her to drink more water, stand up slowly and wear support stockings. He booked a 24-hour tape in two months. He also arranged for her to have a home safety check because of her falls.
h: He advised her to drink more water, stand up slowly and wear support stockings

a.o: Dr. Gamal treated fainting with complete heart block as dehydration.
a.x: Mrs. Shadia should have been admitted for urgent pacing.
a.w: Complete heart block with a slow pulse and fainting can cause sudden death. It needs a pacemaker.

a.o: Dr. Gamal arranged a home safety check.
a.x: This was unnecessary.
a.w: A home safety check helps prevent injury from falls.

a.o: Dr. Gamal checked potassium.
a.x: Potassium was irrelevant.
a.w: High potassium can cause heart block, so checking is right.

a.o: Dr. Gamal noted she takes no heart-slowing drugs.
a.x: That didn't matter.
a.w: Drugs are a common reversible cause of heart block.

s:
Mrs. Khadiga, 66, had a hip replacement nine days ago and has been on enoxaparin injections since. Her platelets were 240 before surgery. Today they were 82. Her left calf became swollen and painful.

She was walking with a frame and eating well. Her wound looked clean and dry, and she had no fever. Dr. Mostafa checked her blood film, which confirmed the low count without clumping, and ordered a leg ultrasound, which showed a clot in the vein behind her knee. Her kidney function was normal.

Mrs. Khadiga said she had never had a clot before, though her sister had one after giving birth. She takes amlodipine for blood pressure and calcium for her bones. She was keen to go home to her husband, who has dementia, and asked how long this would keep her in. Her oxygen was 97 percent and she had no chest pain.

He wrote: "DVT, increase enoxaparin to treatment dose". He asked the nurse to measure her calf every day and booked her physio. He reassured her that the clot was common after hip surgery and was not caused by anything she did.
h: increase enoxaparin to treatment dose

a.o: Dr. Mostafa increased the heparin dose even though Mrs. Khadiga's platelets had halved with a new clot.
a.x: He should have stopped all heparin and started a non-heparin blood thinner like fondaparinux or argatroban.
a.w: A big platelet drop with a new clot 5 to 10 days after heparin is heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. More heparin makes clots worse.

a.o: Dr. Mostafa ordered an ultrasound for a swollen calf.
a.x: An ultrasound was unnecessary.
a.w: An ultrasound confirms a DVT.

a.o: Dr. Mostafa told her the clot was not her fault.
a.x: This reassurance was misleading.
a.w: Reassurance helps her cope; clots after surgery are common.

a.o: Dr. Mostafa booked physio.
a.x: She should rest in bed.
a.w: Moving helps recovery and reduces new clots.

t: No driving advice after an ICD
s:
Mr. Taher, 50, a taxi driver, had an ICD put in after a cardiac arrest from ventricular fibrillation at home. He recovered well and was ready to go home after four days.

His wound was clean and the device check was fine. His echo showed mild weakness of the heart.

He had collapsed while watching football with his family, and his son had started CPR. He had no warning signs before. His coronary angiogram was normal. He was keen to get back to work because he supports his three children and his elderly mother.

Dr. Rehab started him on bisoprolol and ramipril and booked a device check in a month. She showed him how to look after his wound and told him to avoid lifting his left arm above shoulder height for a few weeks. She told him he could go back to work driving his taxi next week as soon as he felt well.
h: She told him he could go back to work driving his taxi next week

a.o: Dr. Rehab told a taxi driver with a new ICD after cardiac arrest he could drive his taxi next week.
a.x: Mr. Taher should have been told not to drive, and that professional driving is usually not allowed after an ICD for cardiac arrest.
a.w: A sudden rhythm or shock while driving could kill him and others. Driving rules after an ICD are strict, especially for professional drivers.

a.o: Dr. Rehab told him to avoid lifting his arm.
a.x: Arm movement was fine.
a.w: Raising the arm above the shoulder can pull the new leads out of place.

a.o: Dr. Rehab started ramipril for a mildly weak heart.
a.x: Ramipril is only for high blood pressure.
a.w: ACE inhibitors protect a weak heart.

a.o: Dr. Rehab booked a device check in a month.
a.x: A check in a year was enough.
a.w: Early checks make sure the device works.

s:
Mr. Osama, 58, had tuberculosis five years ago and was treated. He now has swollen legs, a swollen belly and breathlessness. His neck veins rise when he breathes in instead of falling. His pulse is fast and his blood pressure normal.

Dr. Hamed heard an early knock after the second heart sound. A chest X-ray showed a thin rim of calcium around the heart. The echo showed normal pumping and a septum that bounced with breathing.

He had been feeling tired and breathless for six months. He doesn't drink alcohol. His liver was large and his belly had fluid. His blood pressure dropped a little when he breathed in. His kidney tests were normal, and his BNP was only slightly raised.

Dr. Hamed diagnosed heart failure with a weak heart. He increased furosemide and wrote for a heart failure nurse. He asked the cardiology team to see him and booked a CT of the chest. He asked the dietitian to help him cut down on salt.
h: Dr. Hamed diagnosed heart failure with a weak heart

a.o: Dr. Hamed called it a weak heart when the signs pointed to constrictive pericarditis.
a.x: Mr. Osama should have been worked up for constrictive pericarditis, which can be cured by surgery.
a.w: Old TB, rising neck veins on breathing in, a knock and calcified pericardium with normal pumping mean constriction. It needs pericardiectomy.

a.o: Dr. Hamed booked a chest CT.
a.x: A CT was not needed.
a.w: A CT shows the thickened pericardium.

a.o: Dr. Hamed used furosemide.
a.x: Diuretics should be avoided.
a.w: Gentle diuretics ease swelling while waiting for surgery.

a.o: Dr. Hamed asked the dietitian to help.
a.x: Diet was irrelevant.
a.w: Cutting salt helps any fluid build-up.

t: The wrong first drug for his blood pressure
s:
Mr. Jonathan, 55, is a black man from Jamaica living in Cairo for work. His blood pressure has been above 160/100 on home readings for a month. He has no other illnesses.

He drinks two beers most evenings, walks little and eats a lot of salty takeaway food since moving. He is not diabetic. His kidney tests and urine were normal, and his cholesterol was slightly raised. His ECG showed mild heart strain. He said he would rather take one tablet than several.

Dr. Hany explained the risks of high blood pressure and started ramipril 5 mg daily. He advised him to cut down on salt and alcohol and to walk daily. He booked a blood pressure check in four weeks and asked him to bring his home machine. He wrote the plan in a letter for his GP back home.
h: started ramipril 5 mg daily

a.o: Dr. Hany chose ramipril as the first blood pressure drug for a black man of African-Caribbean descent.
a.x: He should have started amlodipine, a calcium channel blocker.
a.w: In black patients, ACE inhibitors like ramipril work less well on their own; a calcium channel blocker or a thiazide is the preferred first drug.

a.o: Dr. Hany booked the follow-up four weeks later.
a.x: He should have followed up in a year.
a.w: Four weeks is right to check how a new treatment is working.

a.o: Dr. Hany asked him to bring his home machine.
a.x: Home machines should not be trusted.
a.w: Checking a home machine against the clinic one makes the home readings reliable.

a.o: Dr. Hany checked kidneys and urine before treating.
a.x: These tests were not needed.
a.w: Kidney tests and urine checks are part of the first workup.

s:
It was almost five in the afternoon when Mr. Tarek rushed into the ER carrying his nephew Omar, a skinny nine-year-old with a towel pressed to his left arm. Omar had crashed his bicycle into broken glass outside the bakery. By the time they arrived the bleeding had stopped, but the towel was soaked and Omar was pale and crying.

Nurse Salma checked him quickly. His heart was racing at 112, but his blood pressure was fine and he was talking clearly, so she put him in the yellow area. Omar weighed 28 kg, had no allergies his uncle knew of, and had his last tetanus shot at six.

Dr. Hany unwrapped the towel and found a clean 5 cm cut on the inside of the forearm. Omar could move every finger. "We'll need stitches," Dr. Hany said. Mr. Tarek nodded. "His parents are at work, but go ahead, I'm responsible for him." Dr. Hany washed the wound, numbed it with lidocaine and closed it with six neat stitches. He gave Omar 420 mg of paracetamol for the pain and sent him home with his uncle and a wound-care leaflet.
h: "His parents are at work, but go ahead, I'm responsible for him."

a.o: Dr. Hany stitched Omar's arm after only his uncle agreed, when his parents were a phone call away.
a.x: Dr. Hany should have phoned Omar's parents for consent before stitching.
a.w: An uncle is not Omar's legal guardian. The bleeding had stopped, so this was not an emergency and there was time to reach a parent.

a.o: Nurse Salma sent Omar to the yellow area, when a child cut by glass with a racing heart should be seen first.
a.x: Omar should have gone straight to the red area.
a.w: Yellow was right: the bleeding had stopped, his blood pressure was normal and he was talking. A fast heart in a scared, crying child is not shock.

a.o: Dr. Hany gave Omar 420 mg of paracetamol, far too much for a 28 kg boy.
a.x: Omar should have had 280 mg of paracetamol.
a.w: 420 mg is 15 mg/kg for a 28 kg child, a normal dose.

a.o: Omar went home without a tetanus shot after falling on dirty glass.
a.x: Omar should have had a tetanus booster before leaving.
a.w: His last tetanus shot was three years ago. A dirty wound needs a booster only if the last one was more than 5 years ago.
